Note that to make that happen, I´ve also added some arguments, so please check the new help file and may make some adjustments to your code for defining plotting parameters for fixed and surface landmarks. Please give it a go and let me know if something does not work.

You need to install from the Develop branch of geomorph on github, i.e. devtools::install_github("geomorphR/geomorph", ref = "Develop")

Cheers,

Antigoni

However, I am not able yet to test the function because the installment of the latest geomorph package changed my PCA script that is required for the plotspec() visualization. Now I get an error when I try to do a PCA with gm.prcomp() and the symmetric component of shape as input (see attached image). Also, the groups = argument from plotTangentSpace() is absent in gm.prcomp(). Is it possible to incorporate this argument in gm.prcomp()? I was looking if this argument was available in the new function plot.gm.prcomp() which is suggested in the help file of gm.prcomp(), however this function appears to be unrecognizable by R and therefore I was not able to test it (see second attached image).

Maybe you are right in the development with these functions, but these are the things I encounter presently.

Best regards,

Stefan

For this function you will need to wait until the release of the next version of geomorph on CRAN.

As for plotting, group plotting or any other kind of plotting options will be available for that function through calls to basic plot() arguments (e.g. bg = mygroups).

Antigoni

messages.subject: PCA_ellipses
messages.body_plain:
Hi geomorph community,

I am having some type of problem which I do not fully understand. Excuse me my lack of knowledge on this matter, I am still learning how to properly use R/geomorph.

I want to create confidence ellipses in for my PCA, but I did not see an argument for that in "PlotTangentSpace" function so I  have used the package ellipses and ggplot2 to do so. The problem is that when I do so, I get a warning about missing values ( both in geom_point & geom_path).

My question would be, how is it possible that I can perform the PCA using PlotTangetSpace without such a problem (the missing values) and when using the other packages this is not really the case (most of my specimens do not appear). Is it related to how I am writing the code?

Here is my code, if it helps,

# Packages
install.packages("geomorph")
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("ellipse")

# Libraries
library(geomorph)
library(ggplot2)
library(ellipse)

# Importing TPS files
mesem_tps <- readland.tps("mesembrinellidae_TPS.TPS",
                                  negNA = TRUE)

# Data files
Classifier <- read.csv("data/especies.csv",
                       header = TRUE,
                       row.names = 1)
is.factor(Classifier$Sex)
is.factor(Classifier$State)
is.factor(Classifier$Locality)
is.factor(Classifier$Genus)

# Estimating missing landmarks
mesem_est <- estimate.missing(mesem_tps,
                                  method = c("TPS"))
# Generalized Procrustes Analysis
mesem_gpa <- gpagen(mesem_est, PrinAxes = TRUE,
                            max.iter = TRUE,
                            Proj = TRUE,
                            print.progress = TRUE)
plotAllSpecimens(mesem_gpa$coords)

mesem_mshape <- mshape(mesem_gpa$coords)

plot(mesem_mshape)

write.table(mesem_gpa$coords, file = "mesembrinellidae_gpa.csv", sep = ".")

# PCA
groups_Mb <- interaction(Classifier$Species)

col_esp_clas <- rainbow(length(levels(esp_clas)))
mesem_pca <- plotTangentSpace(mesem_gpa$coords, groups = col_esp_clas,
                              legend = TRUE,
                              label = TRUE)

label <- list(expression(italic("E. benoisti")), expression(italic("L. nigripes")),
              expression(italic("M. bellardiana")), expression(italic("M. peregrina")),
              expression(italic("M. bicolor")), expression(italic("E. cyaneicincta")),
              expression(italic("M. batesi")), expression(italic("E. quadrilineata")),
              expression(italic("E. randa")), expression(italic("H. carvalhoi")),
              expression(italic("H. vogelsangi")), expression(italic("H. obscura")),
              expression(italic("A. latifrons")), expression(italic("H. aeneiventris")),
              expression(italic("H. townsendi")), expression(italic("H. cordillera")),
              expression(italic("S. facialis")), expression(italic("H. currani")),
              expression(italic("H. pictipennis")), expression(italic("L. perisi")),
              expression(italic("M. semihyalina")), expression(italic("M. apollinaris"))) #will be used as a label  to the plot
A <- cbind(mesem_pca$pc.scores, esp_clas)
A <- data.frame(A)
A$esp_clas <- as.factor(A$esp_clas)

#definining ellipses to groups (species in this case)
df_ell <- data.frame()
for(g in levels(A$esp_clas)){
  df_ell <- rbind(df_ell, cbind
                  (as.data.frame(with(A[A$esp_clas==g,],
                                      ellipse(cor(PC1, PC2),
                                      scale=c(sd(PC1),sd(PC2)),
                                      centre=c(mean(PC1),mean(PC2))))),
                                      esp_clas=g))}
#pca using ggplot2
pca_ggplot_esp <- ggplot(data = A,
                         aes(x=PC1,
                             y=PC2,
                             colour=esp_clas,
                             shape=esp_clas))+geom_point(size=3)
pca_ggplot_esp <- pca_ggplot_esp+geom_path(data=df_ell,
                                           aes(x=x,
                                               y=y,
                                               colour=esp_clas),
                                               size=0.5,
                                               linetype=2)
pca_ggplot_esp <- pca_ggplot_esp+scale_color_brewer(name="Species",
                                                    labels=label,
                                                    palette = "Dark2")+
  scale_shape_discrete(name="Species", labels=label)
pca_ggplot_esp <- pca_ggplot_esp+theme(axis.text=element_text(size=12),
                                       axis.title=element_text(size=14))+
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 14))+theme(legend.title = element_text(size=16))
plot(pca_ggplot_esp)

Thanks in advance,

--
Diniz Ferreira
Graduando em Ciências Biológicas
Laboratório de Evolução e Genética de Insetos (LEGIN)
DEZG - IB - Universidade Federal de Pelotas

messages.subject: How to construct two-way mixed ANOVA in procD.lm
messages.subject_clean: How to construct two-way mixed ANOVA in procD.lm
messages.body_plain:
Q1: I would like to construct a two-way mixed ANOVA model to test statistical significance of DA and FA. As far as I know, side should be a fixed factor (DA), ind should be a random factor, and their interaction (FA) should be included as well. Without consideration of replication, I can construct the following formula: fit1 <- procD.lm(shape ~ side * ind). Since ind is a random vector, I am thinking to use anova(fit, error = c(...)) to update the denominator for F-value, but which MS should I choose for side, ind, and side:ind? Or maybe am I completely off the correct direction?

Q2: If I wish to incoporate replication into the model, how should I then update the model (fit2 <- procD.lm(shape ~ side...), anova(fit2, error = c()))?

Q3: If I have repeated quantified shape of the same individual during their growth and development 4 times and would like to compare shape changes over time, is the following model correct? fit3 <- procD.lm(shape ~ ind/time), anova(fit3, error = c("ind:time", "Residual")).

The following tables from "FLUCTUATING ASYMMETRY: Measurement, Analysis, Patterns" seems relevant to the construction of fit1 and fit2, in order:

But I am really curious about how to convert them to code in geomorph. My specimen is of object symmetry. Do I need to create a reflected and relabeled copy of shape and combine them for analysis, as did in bilat.symmetry? I do not even know how to trick bilat.symmetry into doing what I want. Without specifying replication, the ind:side is just the residual relabeled and no F-value would be returned to indicate significance of FA. You help is very much appreciated.

Best regards,

Patrick Lv

Patrick,

see the function bilat.symmetry for directly implementing all the (a)symmetry analyses you want in geomorph, that should directly address Q1 and Q2.

Q3 is a whole other matter, but yes, the design you are suggesting seems correct (although you might also want to consider a time-series design, in which case you would need to use a gls approach to incorporate structured error in your model).

Best,

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Hi geomorph community,

I just want to follow up with my question from yesterday, I’m still working on it and I could really appreciate a opinion on that.

I am having some type of problem which I do not fully understand. Excuse me my lack of knowledge on this matter, I am still learning how to properly use R/geomorph.

I want to create confidence ellipses in for my PCA, but I did not see an argument for that in "PlotTangentSpace" function so I  have used the package ellipses and ggplot2 to do so. The problem is that when I do so, I get a warning about missing values ( both in geom_point & geom_path).

My question would be, how is it possible that I can perform the PCA using PlotTangetSpace without such a problem (the missing values) and when using the other packages this is not really the case (most of my specimens do not appear). Is it related to how I am writing the code?

Here is my code, if it helps,

# Packages
install.packages("geomorph")
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("ellipse")

# Libraries
library(geomorph)
library(ggplot2)
library(ellipse)

# Importing TPS files
mesem_tps <- readland.tps("mesembrinellidae_TPS.TPS",
                                  negNA = TRUE)

# Data files
Classifier <- read.csv("data/especies.csv",
                       header = TRUE,
                       row.names = 1)
is.factor(Classifier$Sex)
is.factor(Classifier$State)
is.factor(Classifier$Locality)
is.factor(Classifier$Genus)

# Estimating missing landmarks
mesem_est <- estimate.missing(mesem_tps,
                                  method = c("TPS"))
# Generalized Procrustes Analysis
mesem_gpa <- gpagen(mesem_est, PrinAxes = TRUE,
                            max.iter = TRUE,
                            Proj = TRUE,
                            print.progress = TRUE)
plotAllSpecimens(mesem_gpa$coords)

mesem_mshape <- mshape(mesem_gpa$coords)

plot(mesem_mshape)

write.table(mesem_gpa$coords, file = "mesembrinellidae_gpa.csv", sep = ".")

# PCA
groups_Mb <- interaction(Classifier$Species)

col_esp_clas <- rainbow(length(levels(esp_clas)))
mesem_pca <- plotTangentSpace(mesem_gpa$coords, groups = col_esp_clas,
                              legend = TRUE,
                              label = TRUE)

label <- list(expression(italic("E. benoisti")), expression(italic("L. nigripes")),
              expression(italic("M. bellardiana")), expression(italic("M. peregrina")),
              expression(italic("M. bicolor")), expression(italic("E. cyaneicincta")),
              expression(italic("M. batesi")), expression(italic("E. quadrilineata")),
              expression(italic("E. randa")), expression(italic("H. carvalhoi")),
              expression(italic("H. vogelsangi")), expression(italic("H. obscura")),
              expression(italic("A. latifrons")), expression(italic("H. aeneiventris")),
              expression(italic("H. townsendi")), expression(italic("H. cordillera")),
              expression(italic("S. facialis")), expression(italic("H. currani")),
              expression(italic("H. pictipennis")), expression(italic("L. perisi")),
              expression(italic("M. semihyalina")), expression(italic("M. apollinaris"))) #will be used as a label  to the plot
A <- cbind(mesem_pca$pc.scores, esp_clas)
A <- data.frame(A)
A$esp_clas <- as.factor(A$esp_clas)

#definining ellipses to groups (species in this case)
df_ell <- data.frame()
for(g in levels(A$esp_clas)){
  df_ell <- rbind(df_ell, cbind
                  (as.data.frame(with(A[A$esp_clas==g,],
                                      ellipse(cor(PC1, PC2),
                                      scale=c(sd(PC1),sd(PC2)),
                                      centre=c(mean(PC1),mean(PC2))))),
                                      esp_clas=g))}
#pca using ggplot2
pca_ggplot_esp <- ggplot(data = A,
                         aes(x=PC1,
                             y=PC2,
                             colour=esp_clas,
                             shape=esp_clas))+geom_point(size=3)
pca_ggplot_esp <- pca_ggplot_esp+geom_path(data=df_ell,
                                           aes(x=x,
                                               y=y,
                                               colour=esp_clas),
                                               size=0.5,
                                               linetype=2)
pca_ggplot_esp <- pca_ggplot_esp+scale_color_brewer(name="Species",
                                                    labels=label,
                                                    palette = "Dark2")+
  scale_shape_discrete(name="Species", labels=label)
pca_ggplot_esp <- pca_ggplot_esp+theme(axis.text=element_text(size=12),
                                       axis.title=element_text(size=14))+
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 14))+theme(legend.title = element_text(size=16))
plot(pca_ggplot_esp)

Thanks in advance,
--
Diniz Ferreira
Graduando em Ciências Biológicas
Laboratório de Evolução e Genética de Insetos (LEGIN)
DEZG - IB - Universidade Federal de Pelotas

messages.body_plain:
Diniz,

plotTangentSpace does not provide that plotting functionality. There are many other packages that one can use for plotting confidence ellipses. Since you have estimated missing values in your initial dataset, there are no missing values after GPA. In fact, neither GPA nor plotTangentSpace would work if there were still missing values.

For questions related to ggplot2, please contact the corresponding mailing list, as your questions go beyond the scope of the geomorph mailing list. Here is where to find it: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/

Good luck!

Antigoni

if you have no replicates there is no variance left after the ind:side term has been included to the ind + side, and thus there is no way to calculate statistics for it.

Thank you Antigoni. May I have a follow-up question to your response to my Q3 in the first post.

Recap of Q3: If I have repeatedly quantified shape of the same individual during their growth and development and would like to compare shape changes over time, is the following model correct? fit3 <- procD.lm(shape ~ ind/time), anova(fit3, error = c("ind:time", "Residual")).

Your answer: yes, the design you are suggesting seems correct (although you might also want to consider a time-series design, in which case you would need to use a gls approach to incorporate structured error in your model).

I followed your suggestion and tried to include cov in lm.rrpp to allow for GLS estimation of parameters to account for correlated error structures.

In the example code for lm.rrpp in RRPP user manual, covariance matrix was included into the model as follows:
data(PlethMorph)
fitGLS <- lm.rrpp(TailLength ~ SVL, data = PlethMorph, Cov = PlethMorph$PhyCov, print.progress = FALSE, iter = 999)

I noted that PlethMorph$PhyCov is a 37*37 matrix, whose number of rows equals the length of TailLength and SVL. To explore how I could construct a correlation matrix for my fit3 model, I first learned how such covariance matrix was constructed in nlme package in R:

# This simulated dataset contains 3 repeated measures for 10 individuals.
data <- data.frame(y = rnorm(30), ind = rep(1:10, 3), time = gl(3, 10))
# The 0.8 and 0.4 corresponds to first order parameters for AR (auto-regression) and MA (moving
# average) correlation structure. p=1 and q=1 means only the first order coef are considered.
cs2ARMA <- corARMA(c(0.8, 0.4), form = ~ 1 | ind, p=1, q=1)
cs2ARMA2 <- Initialize(cs2ARMA, data = data)
corMatrix(cs2ARMA2)
# This is the output
# $`1`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`2`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`3`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`4`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`5`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`6`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`7`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`8`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`9`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

# $`10`
#       [,1] [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 1.000 0.88 0.704
# [2,] 0.880 1.00 0.880
# [3,] 0.704 0.88 1.000

It can be seen that all individuals are given the same covariance matrix, which has 3 rows and 3 columns (rather than 30 rows and 30 columns) that account for correlated error structure for 3 repeated measures over time. This makes sense to me. But according to the example code provided by RRPP user manual, the number of rows of the covariance matrix as input for cov argument in lm.rrpp is of the same length as the total number of rows in the whole data (37 individuals, so 37*37 covariance matrix).

In my fit3, if I have 3 repeated measures for each of the 10 individuals, resulting in a total of 30 specimens (the "shape" variable is a 3D list of p*k*30 dimension), what is the appropriate dimension for the covariance matrix if I wish to include cov argument into fit3 to account for correlated error structure? Should it be a 30*30 matrix (since I have 30 specimens in total) or 3*3 matrix (since each ind is measured 3 times)? I would like to construct a matrix of suitable dimension with first order auto-regression and first order moving average error structure.

Thank you.
Patrick

messages.body_plain:
Patrick, the example of RRPP is one of a phylogenetic GPS, i.e. to account for phylogenetic relatedness among species observations while fitting the model. As such, the expected covariance matrix (reflected in the error term) has dimensions that correspond to those of the observations (species values for TailLength and SVL in that example).

Your case is a bit different, as the structured error would be only with respect to the time observations within individuals, not across them. That is, you still expect the individuals to have independent random errors associated, but you may expect the three observations of each individual to be autocorrelated due to the time dimension of your experiment. So this gets a bit complicated.

I guess that for the model to run you would still need a 30x30 matrix, but that matrix would have to accurately reflect the expected structure for your error, i.e. have the matrix you inferred for the time dependence for the blocks within individuals and a structure with ~N(1, 0) across individuals.

But to be honest, I´m not completely sure how that might run in RRPP and if it would actually provide the required output. Maybe Mike can help with that if he has the time.

Cheers,

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
You could attempt to use a Kronecker product to obtain a 30 x 30 matrix that has the 10 3 x 3 identical matrices for individuals.  Using your code, do something like this:

R <- corMatrix(cs2ARMA2)[[1]]

If you have your data arranged as three sets of 10 measurements per individual, then

Cov <- kronecker(R, diag(10))

If you have your data arranged as 10 sets of three measurements, then

Cov <- kronecker(diag(10), R)

Either way works as long as the structure of Cov match the rows of your data.  Your example data used the former approach.  However, the latter approach shows better how a Kronecker product generalizes the 3 x 3 matrix to a 30 x 30 Covariance matrix for all observations (just easier to see with one’s eye what is going on).

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Antigoni and Mike. I understand from Cov <- kronecker(diag(10), R) that the kronecker product produced block diagnoal matrix. I also managed to obtain Cov from the following code:

mats <- corMatrix(cs2ARMA2)
library(Matrix)
mats2 <- bdiag(mats)

Where mats2 is the same as Cov. However, when I tried:

fitGLS1 <- lm.rrpp(y ~ time, data = data, cov = Cov) # I tried Cov from both forms of Kronecker producted as suggested by Mike
anova(fitGLS1)
fitGLS2 <- lm.rrpp(y ~ time, data = data, cov = mats2)
anova(fitGLS2)

Both anova returned identical results to OLS estimation with the following info:
Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares

It can be seen from above that although I specified cov, in neither model the estimation method was GLS. The example in RRPP user manual: fitGLS <- lm.rrpp(TailLength ~ SVL, data = PlethMorph, Cov = PlethMorph$PhyCov, print.progress = FALSE, iter = 999); anova(fitGLS) returned the following info:

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Generalized Least-Squares (via OLS projection)

I am not sure if I missing anything in fitGLS1/2, resulting in OLS estimation although cov is specified? I did not identify how the two models differ from fitGLS. Any idea what I might have missed? Thank you very much for both of your help.

Patrick

On Thursday, 9 April 2020 19:50:30 UTC+8, Michael Collyer wrote:

> You could attempt to use a Kronecker product to obtain a 30 x 30 matrix that has the 10 3 x 3 identical matrices for individuals.  Using your code, do something like this:

>
> If you have your data arranged as three sets of 10 measurements per individual, then
>
> Cov <- kronecker(R, diag(10))
>
> If you have your data arranged as 10 sets of three measurements, then
>
> Cov <- kronecker(diag(10), R)
>
> Either way works as long as the structure of Cov match the rows of your data.  Your example data used the former approach.  However, the latter approach shows better how a Kronecker product generalizes the 3 x 3 matrix to a 30 x 30 Covariance matrix for all observations (just easier to see with one’s eye what is going on).

> Cheers!
> Mike

> > Patrick, the example of RRPP is one of a phylogenetic GPS, i.e. to account for phylogenetic relatedness among species observations while fitting the model. > >
> > Your case is a bit different, as the structured error would be only with respect to the time observations within individuals, not across them. That is, you still expect the individuals to have independent random errors associated, but you may expect the three observations of each individual to be autocorrelated due to the time dimension of your experiment. So this gets a bit complicated.
> >
> > I guess that for the model to run you would still need a 30x30 matrix, but that matrix would have to accurately reflect the expected structure for your error, i.e. have the matrix you inferred for the time dependence for the blocks within individuals and a structure with ~N(1, 0) across individuals.

messages.subject: interpretating shape changes from PCA plots
messages.subject_clean: interpretating shape changes from PCA plots
messages.body_plain:
This might sound like a basic question but it is one that gets asked about from time to time when people look at my results.

How does one interpret shapes from a PCA plot? By eyeballing deformation grids? Is there a more quantitative way of going about this, like the loadings one can look at that to form interpretations?
What is your preferred way?

Nick

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] interpretating shape changes from PCA plots
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] interpretating shape changes from PCA plots
messages.body_plain:
Nick,

A quantitative interpretation of PC loadings requires that each input variable is biologically meaningful and ‘independent’: at least in a biological sense (they will of course be correlated). However, GPA-aligned landmarks or their derivatives (e.g., partial warp scores) are explicitly interdependent, due to the initial GPA of landmarks configurations. As such, interpretation of individual shape variables is not useful, and often incorrect.

Some early GMM papers discuss this in a different context: use of individual shape variables for generating cladistics characters. While the intent was different, the reasons for not interpreting them in this manner are the same.  You will find discussion and examples of the above issues in Rohlf (1998: Syst. Biol.) and Adams and Rosenberg (1998: Syst. Biol.).

Best,

Dean

messages.subject: pairwise error and mixed-design anova question
messages.subject_clean: pairwise error and mixed-design anova question
messages.body_plain:
Hello geomorph community,

I am currently using the function procD.lm to access and test hypothesis and much of it through the example in the help section, the "addition by subtraction" file by Dr. Collyer in the geomorph cran page, as well as the annotated bibliography by the geomorph authors.

I am getting an error which I do not understand: "Error in pairwise(fit.commom, fit.null, groups = data_mesem$Species, print.progress = TRUE) : The groups factor does not have replication at each level."

Question 1) I have been able with the same group to access different things so far, why am I getting this mistake at such point now?

Question 2) I am trying to make pairwise comparisons of shape between both genera and species and I have different specimens numbers throughout my samples (most of these species had not been exhaustively collected and this group has just recently been "established" a family in Diptera). Is there a way to minimize such effects in the mixed-design anova approach?

Here's my code, so far, if it helps:

# models of shape/size variation
data_mesem <- geomorph.data.frame(mesem_gpa,
                                  Species = esp_clas,
                                  Genus = gen_clas)
fit.size <- procD.lm(coords~log(Csize), data = data_mesem,
                     iter = 999,
                     print.progress = TRUE)
fit.spp <- procD.lm(coords~log(Csize)*Species, data = data_mesem,
                    iter = 999,
                    print.progress = TRUE)
fit.gen <- procD.lm(coords~log(Csize)*Species/Genus, data = data_mesem,
                    iter = 999,
                    print.progress = TRUE)
anova(fit.size)
anova(fit.spp)
anova(fit.gen)

#model comparasion
anova(fit.size, fit.spp, fit.gen, print.progress = TRUE)

#commom or unique allometries between genus and species
fit.unique <- procD.lm(coords~log(Csize)*Species/Genus, data = data_mesem,
                       iter = 999,
                       print.progress = TRUE)
fit.commom <- procD.lm(coords~log(Csize)+Species/Genus, data = data_mesem,
                       iter = 999,
                       print.progress = TRUE)
anova(fit.unique)
anova(fit.commom)
anova(fit.commom, fit.unique, print.progress = TRUE) #allometry model selection
reveal.model.designs(fit.commom) #null model
#pairwise comparasions
fit.null <- procD.lm(coords~log(Csize)+Species, data = data_mesem,
                     iter = 999,
                     print.progress = TRUE)
anova(fit.null)
PW_comp <- pairwise(fit.commom, fit.null, groups = data_mesem$Species,
                    print.progress = TRUE)

Any comments on this email is much appreciated,

Thanks in advance,

--
Diniz Ferreira
Graduando em Ciências Biológicas
Laboratório de Evolução e Genética de Insetos (LEGIN)
DEZG - IB - Universidade Federal de Pelotas

Diniz, the error you are getting seems to indicate that there might be species (one or more) for which you only have a single observation. Is this the case?

Regarding the number of specimens across groups in your sample, this should not be an issue (statistically speaking) when using permutation-based inferences as done in geomorph through RRPP (except for the issue mentioned above). But of course, in the moment of interpreting your results, you need to consider from a more philosophical perspective if you trust what you are observing, i.e. in the sense of whether you consider that your samples accurately represent the variation present in nature.

I hope this helps.

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Regarding question 1, you might consider the following:

data_mesem$Species <- factor(data_mesem$Species)

if you have previously culled the species data from a factor that had more levels than what are now represented.  This is a common issue, for example, if originally the data had say 10 species but now only have 8 of the 10 species.  As a factor, the effects of the other two species are still modeled in the model design matrix, which can cause issues.

Regarding everything else, it seems strange that you are nesting genus within species, since each species only has one genus.  Maybe you mean to nest species within genus?  And if you want to do analyses at the level of species, nesting with genus would not be needed, although you might still want to have genus effects in the model; i.e.,

~log(Csize)*Species + log(Csize)* Genus/Species

This is a guess base don my understanding of what you are attempting.  But a model like the one above would allow you to test difference among species while accounting for difference among genera.

Mike

messages.subject: Some questions on shape asymmetry
messages.body_plain:
Hello all. I have some questions on shape asymmetry:

Q1. Why Procrustes variance for asymm.shape is the same as that for FA.component?

library(geomorph)
data(scallops)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = scallops$coorddata, ind=scallops$ind)
scallop.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, object.sym = TRUE,
land.pairs=scallops$land.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 499)

gdf2 <- geomorph.data.frame(shapeasym = scallop.sym$asymm.shape)
asymshapevar <- morphol.disparity(shapeasym ~ 1, groups = NULL, data = gdf2,
                   iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)

gdf3 <- geomorph.data.frame(shapeda = scallop.sym$DA.component)
dashapevar <- morphol.disparity(shapeda ~ 1, groups = NULL, data = gdf3,
                   iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)

gdf4 <- geomorph.data.frame(shapefa = scallop.sym$FA.component)
fashapevar <- morphol.disparity(shapefa ~ 1, groups = NULL, data = gdf4,
                   iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)

I found both asymshapevar and fashapevar to be 0.005128729 and dashapevar to be 0.01965519. Shouldn't variance for asymshapevar be the sum of dashapevar and fashapevar (I am not sure if DA and FA are orthogonal. If not, then asymshapevar should incorporate correlation as well. But in no circumstance should asymshapevar and fashapevar be the same. Where has the contribution of dashapevar gone in asymshapevar)?

Q2. I wish to obtain Procrustes shape coordinates for specimen of object symmetry that includes both symmetric and asymmetric component. I tried two ways.

Method 1: totshape <- scallop.sym$symm.shape + scallop.sym$asymm.shape
Method 2: gpa <- gpagen(scallops$coorddata)
                 totshape2 <- gpa$coords

totshape and totshape2 give different results. Maybe method 1 is incorrect. But any idea why is it wrong?

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

This is probably quite dumb but somehow I cannot figure this out right with the new changes to functions in gemorph/rrpp.

I am trying to do a trajectory analysis, my trajectories are groups (taxa) and my levels are two stages (immature/mature). I have only one observation per level, two per group, so each trajectory is one immature specimen and one mature specimen. I want to do pairwise comparisons of path lengths and angles.

I follow the example of this vignette (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/geomorph/vignettes/geomorph.assistance.html) to adapt my previous script (which worked in geomorph v.3.0.7) but I keep getting the same warning message: ‘The groups factor does not have replication at each level.’

I checked and re-checked but I cannot see what’s going on, am I doing something wrong in  the script. The specimens seem just fine.

For the rest the vignette is quite useful for practitioners to update, thanks for that!

The code:

ONTO <-read.csv("DATA/ONT_SERIES.csv", sep=",",row.names = 1)

##Procrustes coordinates##

coords <- ONTO[,8:81]

coords1 <-(arrayspecs(coords[,1:ncol(coords)], 37,2))#transform data for geomorph.dataframe

#ONTO CATEGORIES#

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Issue with rrpp trajectory.analysis function
messages.body_plain:
If you have n = 1 per level, there is no variance.  If there is no variance, there is no test that can be performed.

You could try the pairwise function to do the analysis you are seeking, but it would merely test if the average path length is significant.  If you want a taxon by taxon comparison, you simply do not have any variance for such a test.  You could merely calculate the distances between individuals as descriptive statistics.  The dist function can do that for you (and you might use the two.d.array function if you have coordinates as data).

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Issue with rrpp trajectory.analysis function
messages.body_plain:
You defined it as one observation per trajectory point.  It is not the number of observations per trajectory but the number of observations per point that have to be greater than 1.  If the error message is not sufficiently the same as lacking variance for you, then you miss the point that in order to have variance, you need to have replication.

Whether version 3.0.7 “worked” is perhaps not relevant.  Some functions will give you results when they shouldn’t.  In older versions, we did not have as many checks for problems.  So it was possible that the function computed results but maybe the results should not have been computed.  Without data and a comparison, I cannot say.  But if you feel comfortable with those results, you are free to install the old version of geomorph and work with it.

Here is the trap (in pairwise, not in trajectory.analysis) that throws the error:

  gp.rep <- by(groups, groups, length)

  if(!all(gp.rep > 1)) stop("The groups factor does not have replication at each level.”)

where “groups" is a factor found from the interaction between groups and traj.points in trajectory.analysis (the trajectory.analysis function uses the pairwise function, so “groups” is the factor for pairwise, which must first be made in trajectory.analysis).  If we did not have this trap, a linear model will still estimate coefficients (even if n = 0), but if n = 0 or 1 for one group level, there is no variance in the particular coefficient estimated; i.e., it is not an estimate.  Just because we might not have prevented this in previous versions does not mean it should not have been prevented and the current version is broken compared to the last.  In fact, we often dealt with users having spurious results for such reasons, which is why we now have such traps.

I hope that helps.

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Issue with rrpp trajectory.analysis function
messages.body_plain:
Because that (pairwise) function does not coerce two group factors — groups and traj.points — into one new factor, like trajectory.analysis does.

We will consider on our next update adding an additional trap to trajectory.analysis so that the error is not triggered in pairwise.  But for your current problem, here is the issue

groups = interaction(groups, traj.pts) # in trajectory analysis

One that step is performed, pairwise will not work.  trajectory.analysis is nothing more than a fancy way to wrap the pairwise function.  You have no interaction because you have no replication of observations at each group x trajectory point level.

Mike

messages.subject: procD.lm and pairwise
messages.body_plain:
Hello Geomorph users,

I am trying to use procD.lm to compare the shapes between the groups in my data set while accounting for sex. In my data I have members from three different artificial selection lines spanning three generations during the selection process (beginning, middle an end). What I am trying to do is pretty simple (I think) I just want to compare the mean shapes of all nine groups. I expect that random bred controls will not differ in shape over the selection process and I expect that none of the founder populations will differ because selection has not been applied. So I concatenate line and generation into a nine level variable using (Line:Generation) called Groups. If I run the code below I get that all 9 groups differ significantly, which is a bit odd if you saw the PCA.

Groups <- Line:Gen

shape_lm <- procD.lm(shape~group, iter = 999, RRPP = T,  SS.type = c("III"),  effect.type = c("F"))
summary(shape_lm)
pw <- pairwise(shape_lm, groups = Groups)
summary(pw, confidence =0.95, test.type = "dist)

If I add sex as a co-variate I will get one or more groups differs significantly and sex accounts for a small but significant amount of variation. However, if I now take this new model with the co-variate and put it into pairwise() I get a response that says no groups differ despite what the summary of the procD.lm says. The code is written out below.

shape_lm_2 <- procD.lm(shape~group + sex, iter = 999, RRPP = T,  SS.type = c("III"),  effect.type = c("F")) )
summary(shape_lm_2)
pw_2 <- pairwise(shape_lm_2, groups = Groups)
summary(pw_2, confidence =0.95, test.type = "dist)

I am pretty new to morphometrics and multivariate stats I am finding the vignette/ help are a bit inaccessible. I think the problem might be something to do with the null that pairwise is using? Reveal.model.designs(shape_lm_2) tells me this, but I am not sure how to interpret it:

           Reduced         Full
group      sex         group + sex
sex        group       group + sex  <-  Null/Full inherent in pairwise

Any insights would be greatly appreciated! If anyone has advice or could suggest some reading I could do that would be awesome!

Cheers,
Cole

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] procD.lm and pairwise
messages.body_plain:
Cole,

The issue is that you did not define a null model in your pairwise test, so the function must use what it thinks could be the null model based on your procD.lm fit.  In this case, it used an illogical model.  The reveal.model.designs function tells you which null model/full model comparison pairwise will use if you leave it up to the function to guess.  Even though you used type III SS, it uses the order of variables to guess.  In your case the null model has group as a factor and the full model, group + sex as factors.  Therefore, you are testing for group differences after holding group variation constant.  There is no way to find a significant test result that way.

You can do one of two things.

1) Create another procD.lm fit with shape ~ sex, and define this as the null model in pairwise
2) Change the order in shape_lm_2 to be shape ~ sex + group

The second option merely tricks pairwise; the first option means you take control of defining what the null model should be.

The reason that a null model does not have to be defined in pairwise is that it is computationally quite a bit faster if you can rely on the random outcomes already generated from procD.lm.  Generally speaking, that might work well with type I SS and some a priori reasoning given to term order; it is less-straightforward with type III SS.  It is always best to define the null model so you know exactly on which expectation — like sexual dimorphism — you are conditioning your results.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.subject: FA calculation internally in bilat.symmetry
messages.body_plain:
Hello Geomorph users,

I am looking into the source code for bilat.symmetry in geomorph v3.2.1 to understand how FA is calculated internally in bilat.symmetry.

The source code for bilat.symmetry contains the following code snippet:

mn.DA <- DA.mns[, , 1] - DA.mns[, , 2]
...
FA.component <- simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j) {
    t(matrix(FA.component[j, ], k, p)) + mn.shape - mn.DA
}))

It can be seen that mn.DA refers to difference between 1st and 2nd configuration in DA.mns. DA.mns is the DA.component in bilat.symmetry output where the first 2 configurations are original and relabeled reflections of the 1st specimen. That means FA is calculated for all specimens by the difference between relabed reflection of each specimen and its original configuration plus mean shape of original and relabled reflections of all specimens minus difference between original and relabeled reflections of the 1st specimen.

Based on example data and source code, I replicated bilat.symmetry results:

library(geomorph)
data(scallops)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = scallops$coorddata, ind=scallops$ind)

A <- gpagen(scallops$coorddata)
size <- A$Csize
A <- A$coords
n <- dim(A)[3]
k <- dim(A)[2]
p <- dim(A)[1]
ind <- scallops$ind
nind <- nlevels(ind)
land.pairs <- scallops$land.pairs
npairs <- nrow(land.pairs)
A2 <- A
A2[land.pairs[, 1], , ] <- A[land.pairs[, 2], , ]
A2[land.pairs[, 2], , ] <- A[land.pairs[, 1], , ]
A2[, 1, ] <- A2[, 1, ] * (-1)
A_long <- array(c(A, A2), c(p, k, 2 * n))
ind <- factor(rep(ind, 2))
side <- gl(2, n)
gpa.res <- gpagen(A_long)
A_long <- gpa.res$coords

# Table specifying ordering of specimens
# row A_long scallop.sym$DA.component
# 1 ind1 ind1
# 2 ind2 ind1RelabledReflection
# 3 ind3 ind2
# 4 ind4 ind2RelabledReflection
# 5 ind5 ind3
# 6 ind1RelabledReflection ind3RelabledReflection
# 7 ind2RelabledReflection ind4
# 8 ind3RelabledReflection ind4RelabledReflection
# 9 ind4RelabledReflection ind5
# 10         ind5RelabledReflection ind6RelabledReflection

scallop.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, object.sym = TRUE,
land.pairs=scallops$land.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 499)

# FA for the 1st specimen (scallop.sym$DA.component is equivalent to the DA.mns used in source code)
fa_a1 <- A_long[,,6] - A_long[,,1] + mshape(A_long) -
(scallop.sym$DA.component[,,1] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,2])

# FA for the 4th specimen
fa_a4 <- A_long[,,9] - A_long[,,4] + mshape(A_long) -
(scallop.sym$DA.component[,,1] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,2]) # Not (scallop.sym$DA.component[,,8] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,7])

fa_a1 and fa_a4 are identical to scallop.sym$FA.component[,,1] and scallop.sym$FA.component[,,4], respectively. So I can confirm that bilat.symmetry uses difference between the 1st specimen and its relabled reflection in calculation of FA for all specimens. I do not understand why the difference between original and relabled reflection of the first specimen is subtracted when calculating FA for each specimen. I can understand adding mn.shape to t(matrix(FA.component[j, ], k, p)) allows for more meaningful interpretation and visualization. But why mn.DA is subtracted where mn.DA concerns itself with only the first specimen? The first specimen is so arbitrary.

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] FA calculation internally in bilat.symmetry

Hello Geomorph users,

I am looking into the source code for bilat.symmetry in geomorph v3.2.1 to understand how FA is calculated internally in bilat.symmetry.

The source code for bilat.symmetry contains the following code snippet:

mn.DA <- DA.mns[, , 1] - DA.mns[, , 2]

...

FA.component <- simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j) {

    t(matrix(FA.component[j, ], k, p)) + mn.shape - mn.DA

}))

It can be seen that mn.DA refers to difference between 1st and 2nd configuration in DA.mns. DA.mns is the DA.component in bilat.symmetry output where the first 2 configurations are original and relabeled reflections of the 1st specimen. That means FA is calculated for all specimens by the difference between relabed reflection of each specimen and its original configuration plus mean shape of original and relabled reflections of all specimens minus difference between original and relabeled reflections of the 1st specimen.

Based on example data and source code, I replicated bilat.symmetry results:

library(geomorph)

data(scallops)

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = scallops$coorddata, ind=scallops$ind)

A <- gpagen(scallops$coorddata)

size <- A$Csize

A <- A$coords

n <- dim(A)[3]

k <- dim(A)[2]

p <- dim(A)[1]

ind <- scallops$ind

nind <- nlevels(ind)

land.pairs <- scallops$land.pairs

npairs <- nrow(land.pairs)

A2 <- A

A2[land.pairs[, 1], , ] <- A[land.pairs[, 2], , ]

A2[land.pairs[, 2], , ] <- A[land.pairs[, 1], , ]

A2[, 1, ] <- A2[, 1, ] * (-1)

A_long <- array(c(A, A2), c(p, k, 2 * n))

ind <- factor(rep(ind, 2))

side <- gl(2, n)

gpa.res <- gpagen(A_long)

A_long <- gpa.res$coords

# Table specifying ordering of specimens

# row   A_long                                                scallop.sym$DA.component

# 1                   ind1                                                     ind1

# 2                   ind2                                                     ind1RelabledReflection

# 3                   ind3                                                     ind2

# 4                   ind4                                                     ind2RelabledReflection

# 5                   ind5                                                     ind3

# 6                   ind1RelabledReflection            ind3RelabledReflection

# 7                   ind2RelabledReflection          ind4

# 8                   ind3RelabledReflection            ind4RelabledReflection

# 9                   ind4RelabledReflection          ind5

# 10             ind5RelabledReflection            ind6RelabledReflection

scallop.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, object.sym = TRUE,

land.pairs=scallops$land.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 499)

# FA for the 1st specimen (scallop.sym$DA.component is equivalent to the DA.mns used in source code)

fa_a1 <- A_long[,,6] - A_long[,,1] + mshape(A_long) -

                        (scallop.sym$DA.component[,,1] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,2])

# FA for the 4th specimen

fa_a4 <- A_long[,,9] - A_long[,,4] + mshape(A_long) -

                        (scallop.sym$DA.component[,,1] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,2]) # Not (scallop.sym$DA.component[,,8] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,7])

fa_a1 and fa_a4 are identical to scallop.sym$FA.component[,,1] and scallop.sym$FA.component[,,4], respectively. So I can confirm that bilat.symmetry uses difference between the 1st specimen and its relabled reflection in calculation of FA for all specimens. I do not understand why the difference between original and relabled reflection of the first specimen is subtracted when calculating FA for each specimen. I can understand adding mn.shape to t(matrix(FA.component[j, ], k, p)) allows for more meaningful interpretation and visualization. But why mn.DA is subtracted where mn.DA concerns itself with only the first specimen? The first specimen is so arbitrary.

Thanks.

YF Wen

messages.subject: Re: interpretation of centroid size
messages.body_plain:
Centroid size is not an absolute measure of size at all. It will be entirely dependent on the landmarks you choose to represent the structure, and it will change accordingly.

How well it correlates with the body size or the relative to body size is something you need to investigate. There is no definitive answer for that.

You might start with a simple correlation or a regression analysis.

messages.subject: Re: interpretation of centroid size
messages.body_plain:
It is somewhat unclear to me what you want to do. Are you interested in studying the allometric scaling of bill size with respect to body size? And also what is your measure of body size (weight?, volume? cranio-caudal length?, some sort of surface area?). The dimensions of  the input data will determine how you interpret the coefficients from that regression, i.e., whether your hard-seed eating groups have bills indeed relatively big for their body size.

If your goal is to study allometric relationship between bill shape and bill size, then you would generally do an regression of log(centroid size) on procrustes coordinates. If you want to study the shape patterns in groups after that relationship is accounted for then you would use the residuals from that regression. procD.lm() is the function in the geomorph to do that. Alternatively for the shape allometry model, as the size measure you can opt to use directly the body size, as oppose the centroid size of your bill landmarks.

messages.subject: Re: interpretation of centroid size
messages.body_plain:
So in the realm of traditional morphometrics, it is somewhat unusual to use centroid size as a measure of size. Because unlike physical traits like weight, height, length, cross-section, volume, centroid size is not just the property of an individual, but also depends on landmarks chosen. As such, while it can have a unit like mm, it is not a fixed value and will only exist in the context of that analysis. I don't know how many landmarks you have, but take randomly half of them out and recalculate the centroid size, and repeat a few times, and you will see the value, and possibly the relationship, change.

You said you have 3D data. Perhaps calculating volumes of bill, or surface areas might be a more prudent approach?

Regardless, what you describe seems correct -with the caveat above- to me.

El lun., 13 abr. 2020 a las 16:41, Mike Collyer (<mlco...@gmail.com>) escribió:

> Because that (pairwise) function does not coerce two group factors — groups and traj.points — into one new factor, like trajectory.analysis does.
>
> We will consider on our next update adding an additional trap to trajectory.analysis so that the error is not triggered in pairwise.  But for your current problem, here is the issue
>
> groups = interaction(groups, traj.pts) # in trajectory analysis
>
> One that step is performed, pairwise will not work.  trajectory.analysis is nothing more than a fancy way to wrap the pairwise function.  You have no interaction because you have no replication of observations at each group x trajectory point level.
>
> Mike
>
> > On Apr 13, 2020, at 11:00 AM, Guillermo Navalón <guiye...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Also, I conducted allometric pairwise comparisons with the same data and worked like a charm.

> > > Also, why if the issue concerns variance the warning is about correspondence of levels?
> > >
> > > Thank you for your assistance,
> > >
> > > Guille
> > >
> > > El lun., 13 abr. 2020 a las 14:56, Mike Collyer (<mlco...@gmail.com>) escribió:
> > > > If you have n = 1 per level, there is no variance.  If there is no variance, there is no test that can be performed.
> > > >
> > > > You could try the pairwise function to do the analysis you are seeking, but it would merely test if the average path length is significant.  If you want a taxon by taxon comparison, you simply do not have any variance for such a test.  You could merely calculate the distances between individuals as descriptive statistics.  The dist function can do that for you (and you might use the two.d.array function if you have coordinates as data).

Dear Prof. Dean, thank you for posting updated code. There is still one thing that I do not particularly understand in the updated code. Calculation of total asymmetry and FA involved relabled reflection minus original specimen:

asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[indsq,] - avg.side.symm[-indsq,]
FA.component <- ind.mns[indsq,] - ind.mns[-indsq,]

Since indsq <- seq(n.side, (n.ind*n.side), n.side), I could tell [indsq,] extracts 2nd, 4th, 6th, ... specimen, which are relabled reflections of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, ... specimen. So total asymmetry and FA involved relabled reflection minus original specimen. In contrast, DA is estimated as follows in updated source code:

mn.DA <- matrix(apply((DA.est[-indsq,] - DA.est[indsq,]),2,mean),byrow=T,nrow=p,ncol=k)

This means DA is obtained by original specimen minus relabeled reflections, the reverse of the direction in which total asymmetry and FA is obtained.

The above code can be translated into the following table:

Original   RelabledReflection      TotalAsymmetry   DA   FA        ReasonableFA
3.2 2      2 - 3.2 = -1.2 ((3.2-2)  + (5.1- 4) + (9.8 - 9) + (12.9-12))/4 = 1 -1.2 - 1 = -2.2 0.2
5.1 4      4 - 5.1 = -1.1 ((3.2-2)  + (5.1- 4) + (9.8 - 9) + (12.9-12))/4 = 1 -1.1 - 1 = -2.1 0.1
9.8 9      9 - 9.8 = -0.8 ((3.2-2)  + (5.1- 4) + (9.8 - 9) + (12.9-12))/4 = 1 -0.8 - 1 = -1.8 -0.2
12.9        12      12 - 12.9 = -0.9         ((3.2-2)  + (5.1- 4) + (9.8 - 9) + (12.9-12))/4 = 1 -0.9 - 1 = -1.9 -0.1

It seems that FA column above is not what is meant by definition of FA. In contrasts, the ReasonableFA column is what we want, which seems cannot be obtained following the ways in which total asymmetry, DA, and FA were calculated in the code. I am not sure if I have missed any part of the code.

Thank you again for your help.

YF Wen

DA.mns is the DA.component in bilat.symmetry output where the first 2 configurations are original and relabeled reflections of the 1st specimen. That means FA is calculated for all specimens by the difference between relabed reflection of each specimen and its original configuration plus mean shape of original and relabled reflections of all specimens minus difference between original and relabeled reflections of the 1st specimen.

>
>

>

>

>
> A_long <- array(c(A, A2), c(p, k, 2 * n))

> ind <- factor(rep(ind, 2))
>

>
> gpa.res <- gpagen(A_long)

> A_long <- gpa.res$coords

>
>

>
> # 6                   ind1RelabledReflection            ind3RelabledReflection
>
> # 7                   ind2RelabledReflection          ind4
>
> # 8                   ind3RelabledReflection            ind4RelabledReflection
>
> # 9                   ind4RelabledReflection          ind5
>
> # 10             ind5RelabledReflection            ind6RelabledReflection
>
>
>
> scallop.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, object.sym = TRUE,
>
> land.pairs=scallops$land.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 499)
>
>
>
> # FA for the 1st specimen (scallop.sym$DA.component is equivalent to the DA.mns used in source code)
>
> fa_a1 <- A_long[,,6] - A_long[,,1] + mshape(A_long) -
>
>                         (scallop.sym$DA.component[,,1] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,2])
>
>
>
> # FA for the 4th specimen
>
> fa_a4 <- A_long[,,9] - A_long[,,4] + mshape(A_long) -
>
>                         (scallop.sym$DA.component[,,1] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,2]) # Not (scallop.sym$DA.component[,,8] - scallop.sym$DA.component[,,7])
>
>
>
> fa_a1 and fa_a4 are identical to scallop.sym$FA.component[,,1] and scallop.sym$FA.component[,,4], respectively. So I can confirm that bilat.symmetry uses difference between the 1st specimen and its relabled reflection in calculation of FA for all specimens. I do not understand why the difference between original and relabled reflection of the first specimen is subtracted when calculating FA for each specimen. I can understand adding mn.shape to t(matrix(FA.component[j, ], k, p)) allows for more meaningful interpretation and visualization. But why mn.DA is subtracted where mn.DA concerns itself with only the first specimen? The first specimen is so arbitrary.
>
>
>
> Thanks.
>
>
>
> YF Wen

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was wondering if anyone had any input about why the p-values shown in the output from my procD.lm do not change even when I change/ add in new terms to the model? The other values (MS, Rsq, Z etc.) change however, all of the p-values always remain the exact same. Just curious as to why this may be as it seems really odd.

Thanks!
Chelsea

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] procD.lm output
messages.body_plain:
Chelsea,

This is a guess without additional information about SS.type, but if you are adding terms sequentially, Z-scores based on F-values can change (because the Residual SS changes) but the rank order of the values in the random permutations might stay the same, so the P-values do not change.  I would not expect SS, MS, or Rsq to change with SS.type = “I” and no order of terms changed, unless you are targeting on Residuals, which will naturally change because of additional terms.

Note also that P-values depend on the number of permutations and the seed used.  Without making changes to these, the value will stay the same with re-analysis (because the set of random permutations is the same).

What would be really odd is if when adding more terms, sequentially, P-values changed for the first terms in the model.  If you use conditional (type = II) or marginal (type = III) SS, the expectation of P-value constancy when adding more terms would be odd, as in these cases effects are conditioned on other effects.

Hope that helps! -Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] procD.lm output
messages.body_plain:
OK, with that in mind, if you add more terms to a model, you change the SS. MS, and Rsq for terms that were already in the model because the SS is calculated with respect to other terms in the model, which has changed.  So let’s say this has the effect of reducing SS for term A.  If it decreases SS for term A in a similar way in every random permutation, the rank of the observed SS in the distribution of random SS might not change at all, so the P-value stays the same.

A Z-score is based on the dispersion of the sampling distribution of the statistic used (F by default).  P-values only consider the rank of values.  So P-values might be less sensitive to changes.

I do wish to emphasize strongly to all reading this that I am not saying P-values should be the same, no matter what.  There is a logical reason that they could stay the same; there is also possible ways for them to change.   It depends on many things, like the size of effect, interaction of effects, etc.

Cheers!
Mike

Prof. Dean, thank you for the effort.

For everyone,

I noted from a recent paper by Gunz (Sci Adv. 2020;6(7):eaax9935) that magnitude of fluctuating asymmetry can be quantified as the Procrustes distance between each individual and its relabled reflection after DA has been removed. I want to know how to remove DA, which is a configuration made of Procrustes shape coordinates, from Procrustes distance, which is a single value. I tried:

# Define the function that calculates angle in radian. For Procrustes-aligned shape coordinates, this is mathematically equivalent to Procurstes distance (CS set to 1, angle in radian equals arch length in shape space)
angle.calc <- function (x, y)
{
    x <- as.vector(x)/sqrt(sum(x^2))
    y <- as.vector(y)/sqrt(sum(y^2))
    rho <- acos((sum((x - y)^2) - 2)/-2)
    return(rho)
}

# Procrustes distance between 1st individual and its relabled reflection
totasym_score <- angle.calc(A_long[,,1],  A_long[,,6])

# Now I tried to remove DA and calculate magnitude of FA
mean_symm <- mshape(A_long)

mean_DA <- matrix(apply((two.d.array(scallop.sym$DA.component)[seq(2, 10, 2),] -
     two.d.array(scallop.sym$DA.component)[seq(1, 10, 2),]),
2, mean),
  byrow = T, nrow = 46, ncol = 3)

DAtoSymm <- angle.calc(mean_DA, mean_symm)

fa_score_a1 <- totasym_score - DAtoSymm

I calculated Procrustes distance between mean of the symmetric component of the specimen and DA. This distance, DAtoSymm, was then subtracted from totasym_score. I am not sure if my method is correct. If yes, the fa_score_a1 yielded a value of -1.414422, I do not know how I could interprete this negative value. If not, can anyone help with the correct code?

Thans again.

YF Wen

messages.body_plain:
I read Mardia and Bookstein's paper "Statistical assessment of bilateral symmetry of shapes" and made some progress in understanding method to calculate FA. However, I get different results based on formula provided in this paper.

Equation 3.2 in Mardia's paper is most relevant to how individual magnitude of FA is calculated:

In this formula, X^P and Y^P are Procrustes shape coordinates for original and relabled reflection of all specimens, respectively. X_bar and Y_bar are the mean shape of all X^P and Y^P, respectively. D^2 is squared Procrustes distance between two configurations, which is calculated in squared Euclidean distance. It can be calculated using the dist function, which is how geomorph calculates Procrustes distance.

Using the scallop data from geomorph, I tried to calculate magnitude of FA for the 1st specimen in the dataset following Mardia's equation. You may directly copy and paste the code to replicate my results.

library(geomorph)

library(Morpho)

data(scallops)

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = scallops$coorddata, ind=scallops$ind)

# Code adapted from bilat.symmetry source code

A <- gpagen(scallops$coorddata)

size <- A$Csize

A <- A$coords

n <- dim(A)[3]

k <- dim(A)[2]

p <- dim(A)[1]

ind <- scallops$ind

nind <- nlevels(ind)

land.pairs <- scallops$land.pairs

npairs <- nrow(land.pairs)

A2 <- A

A2[land.pairs[, 1], , ] <- A[land.pairs[, 2], , ]

A2[land.pairs[, 2], , ] <- A[land.pairs[, 1], , ]

A2[, 1, ] <- A2[, 1, ] * (-1)

A_long <- array(c(A, A2), c(p, k, 2 * n))

ind <- factor(rep(ind, 2))

side <- gl(2, n)

gpa.res <- gpagen(A_long)

# A_long below contains Procrustes shape coordinates for all original specimens and

# their relabled reflections. Ordering of specimens can be understood through the

# table in the first post of this thread (15 Apr)

A_long <- gpa.res$coords

############################ Total asymmetry for the 1st specimen####################################

TotAsym_score_s1 <- dist(two.d.array(A_long[,,c(1, 6)]))

############################ Magnitude of DA for the 1st specimen#########################################

mean_Original <- mshape(A_long[,,c(1:5)])

mean_RelabRefl <- mshape(A_long[,,c(6:10)])

OriginalRelabRefl <- bindArr(mean_Original, mean_RelabRefl, along = 3)

DA_score <- dist(two.d.array(OriginalRelabRefl))

#######################  FA score calculation using 2 methods ##############################

# Method 1 for calculating FA score: total asymmetry minus DA

FA_score1a_s1 <- sqrt(TotAsym_score_s1^2 - DA_score^2)

FA_score1b_s1 <- TotAsym_score_s1 - DA_score

# Method 2 for calculating FA score: by Madria's algorithm for FA

diff_Orginal_meanOriginal_s1 <- A_long[,,1] - mean_Original

diff_RelabRefl_meanRelabRefl_s1 <- A_long[,,6] - mean_RelabRefl

diff_both_s1 <- bindArr(diff_Orginal_meanOriginal_s1, diff_RelabRefl_meanRelabRefl_s1, along = 3)

FA_score2_s1 <- dist(two.d.array(diff_both_s1))

Method 1 above obtained FA by total asymmetry minus DA. Two FA scores are listed since I am not sure whether squared distance or distance should be used during calculation. Method 2 obtained FA according to formula for FA shown in the figure above. FA_score1a_s1, FA_score1b_s1, and FA_score2_s1 are different. I must be wrong somewhere but I cannot figure out. I think method 1 and 2 should give identical value if calculated in the same way. So I think I must wrong somewhere. I know MorphoJ could do the calculation automatically. But I wish to know the steps behind. Coding by myself helps. I guess I am close to the answer. I would be very much appreciated if anyone could comment on the code, or directly answer by coding. Thank you.

Best regards,

YF Wen

messages.body_plain:
In geomorph vignette "Addition by subtraction", there is the following code:
fit.common <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + treatment/family, data = gdf, print.progress = FALSE)
Since family is a random effect nested within the fixed effect treatment, main effect of treatment is tested with updated F-value denominator MS_Treatment:Family.

I am wondering if every family received each level of treatment, i.e., treatment and family are crossed rather than nested, but family is still a random effect, how should I rewirte fit.common.
Is fit.common2 <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + treatment*family, data = gdf) correct? How should I update denominator for all terms?

If I have only one fixed effect of treatment and want to consider all specimens as random realization of all possible samples of the same size, how should I test the effect of treatment? fit <- procD.lm(coords ~ treatment) is what is normally done but this does not seem to reflect the random nature of the specimens.

Thanks.

Kieran

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Procrustes ANOVA for two crossed factors with one being random
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Procrustes ANOVA for two crossed factors with one being random
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kieran,

You are correct that if every family received every level of treatment, you can set up your linear model either with crossing or nesting.  Here is how to do it either way:

 fit.common2 <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + family * treatment, data = gdf) # crossing

 fit.common2 <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + family + treatment/family, data = gdf) # nesting

Using type II or type III SS will produce the same SS with either model above; using type I SS will alter the SS, based on term order.  (The columns of the design matrix are the same in both cases but not in the same order.)

You could perform ANOVA as

anova(fit.common2)

but the test for treatment might not be appropriate, as it assumes all terms are fixed.  You can do something, like

anova(fit.common2, error = c(“Residuals”, “Residuals”, “family:treatment”, “Residuals”)

to adjust the F values of treatment to be calculated with respect to random effects, rather than residuals.  This is explained in the vignette but note that it was based on the formula you originally used.  The point is that the solution is not in how you set up the formula but how you adjust the F values in ANOVA.

Hope that helps.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hello Geomorph community,

I have a little question on Repeatability calculation :)
So, in my dataset are 277 specimens, each one was digitized twice (which means replicates=2). I want to compute repeatability value. Firstly, I read guide from Dr. Sherratt and then this disscusion in geomorph google group (https://groups.google.com/forum/m/#!topic/geomorph-r-package/Cj_CfXzJtrw).
I did a nested ANOVA:

id=gl(2,277)
geomorphdataframe=geomorph.data.frame(Shape=Shape,
+                                       ind=id,
+                                       indiv=Specimen_info$individual_names
+                                       rep=as.factor(Specimen_info$rep)
+ )
anv<-procD.lm(Shape ~ ind, data = geomorphdataframe, iter = 999)
summary(anv)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

           Df      SS       MS     Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)
ind:rep     1 0.03971 0.039707 0.02564 14.527 4.4738  0.001 **
Residuals 552 1.50879 0.002733 0.97436
Total     553 1.54850
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: procD.lm(f1 = Shape ~ ind:rep, data = geomorphdataframe)

So, my Repeatability in this case is:

(MS(ind:rep) - MS(residuals)) / (MS(ind:rep) + MS(residuals))

Can someone tell me if the formula is correct on not? :)

Then I was surprised that all individuals are in resudials, so I decided to make procD.lm in a little different way:

geomorphdataframe=geomorph.data.frame(Shape=Shape,
+                                       ind=id,
+                                       indiv=Specimen_info$individual_names

+ )
anv_indiv<-procD.lm(Shape ~ indiv, data = geomorphdataframe, iter = 999)
summary(anv_indiv)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization

Number of permutations: 1000

So, my Repeatability in this case is:

(MS(indiv) - MS(residuals)) / (MS(indiv) + MS(residuals))

Can someone explaine to me which one procD.lm formula is correct?

Thank you in advance!
Lyna

messages.body_plain:
Kieran,

Sorry, I missed your follow up question.  There really is no difference in the two styles.  In fact, R has a particular way of expanding equations.

~ a * b

is expanded to

~ a + b + a:b

and

~ a/b

is expanded to

~ a + a:b

If you expand the equation on your own, using ~ a + b + a/b, this is what R does:

> terms(~ a + b + a/b)
~a + b + a/b
attr(,"variables")
list(a, b)
attr(,"factors")
  a b a:b
a 1 0   1
b 0 1   1
attr(,"term.labels")
[1] "a"   "b"   "a:b"
attr(,"order")
[1] 1 1 2
attr(,"intercept")
[1] 1
attr(,"response")
[1] 0
attr(,".Environment")
<environment: R_GlobalEnv>

Meaning, that R changes a/b to a:b.  They are the same.  Your concern with notation has no implication for the results.  But, concerning your notation, you are right that we should probably use ind:side or side:ind (again the same), since this is how R changes it.

Regarding nesting more generally, I think assigning “fixed” or “random” terms to a design like this can be misleading (I think both are random effects).  I found the following that might help explain the concept (using lme4):

https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/228800/crossed-vs-nested-random-effects-how-do-they-differ-and-how-are-they-specified

There is a good demonstration for the difference between nested and crossed designs, with the caveat, "Nesting is a property of the data, or rather the experimental design, not the model.”  In the example, there is a design where data are collected from classes nested within schools.  Even if class 1 = math and class 2 = literature, taught at each school, class is still nested within school rather than school nested within class, even though doing either could result in the same model, depending on other terms in the model.  Likewise, left sides or right sides are inherent attributes of individuals.  I try to think of it in a hierarchal context rather than forcing a “fixed” label on some part of it.  Thus, ind/side demonstrates the hierarchy.

Nevertheless, I would agree that ind:side or side:ind is more precise to inform the model rather than the design and something we should consider.

Thanks for provoking this!

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Lyna,

In general, assessing repeatability is accomplished using some variant of the intraclass correlation; which is a ratio of variance among individuals as compared to total variation. The simplest model would be:

R = S_a^2 / (S_a^2+S_w^2)

Where S_a^2 is the among individual variance and S_w^2 is the within individual variance. These values are obtained from an ANOVA table where variation is partitioned. Doing this properly requires matching the data that one has with the model being used. I suggest a careful reading of the primary literature to sort that out for your particular case (e.g., Arnqvist and Martensson 1998 is a good place to start).

Note that Em’s post is based on the logic espoused in this, and related papers. She could speak to your specific question.

Best,

Dean

On Friday, April 17, 2020 at 12:59:00 PM UTC-2:30, Michael Collyer wrote:

> OK, with that in mind, if you add more terms to a model, you change the SS. MS, and Rsq for terms that were already in the model because the SS is calculated with respect to other terms in the model, which has changed.  So let’s say this has the effect of reducing SS for term A.  If it decreases SS for term A in a similar way in every random permutation, the rank of the observed SS in the distribution of random SS might not change at all, so the P-value stays the same.
>
> A Z-score is based on the dispersion of the sampling distribution of the statistic used (F by default).  P-values only consider the rank of values.  So P-values might be less sensitive to changes.
>
> I do wish to emphasize strongly to all reading this that I am not saying P-values should be the same, no matter what.  There is a logical reason that they could stay the same; there is also possible ways for them to change.   It depends on many things, like the size of effect, interaction of effects, etc.
>
> Cheers!

> Mike
>

> > On Apr 17, 2020, at 11:03 AM, Chelsea Bishop <chelseae...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Thanks Mike this does help. Sorry, I forgot to add that the SS type = II.
> >
> > On Friday, April 17, 2020 at 12:12:06 PM UTC-2:30, Michael Collyer wrote:
> > > Chelsea,
> > >
> > > This is a guess without additional information about SS.type, but if you are adding terms sequentially, Z-scores based on F-values can change (because the Residual SS changes) but the rank order of the values in the random permutations might stay the same, so the P-values do not change.  I would not expect SS, MS, or Rsq to change with SS.type = “I” and no order of terms changed, unless you are targeting on Residuals, which will naturally change because of additional terms.
> > >
> > > Note also that P-values depend on the number of permutations and the seed used.  Without making changes to these, the value will stay the same with re-analysis (because the set of random permutations is the same).
> > >
> > > What would be really odd is if when adding more terms, sequentially, P-values changed for the first terms in the model.  If you use conditional (type = II) or marginal (type = III) SS, the expectation of P-value constancy when adding more terms would be odd, as in these cases effects are conditioned on other effects.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Can i use geomorph even if i have non-homologous points ?
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Can i use geomorph even if i have non-homologous points ?
messages.body_plain:
Coline,

You are correct that pseudo-points, or equally spaced points along a curve, are not homologous in the sense that type I landmarks are.  That is because the biological homology statement here rests with the curve itself, not the points.

However, if all curves have the same starting point, and all have the same number of points in the same order, one may treat them as sliding semilandmarks for the purposes of the analysis. There is a rather large literature on how and why such methods are useful, but suffice it to say that for comparing the shapes of curves this is one path forward.

One may perform this analysis in geomorph: please see the help files and vignettes.

Best,

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

https://www.eeob.iastate.edu/faculty/adams/

phone: 515-294-3834

From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of Coline Verot
Sent: Monday, April 27, 2020 12:43 PM
To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Can i use geomorph even if i have non-homologous points ?

Hi !!

I have to analyze the variations of molar shapes between several specimens. To do this i use tpsDig/Util to create the outline of molars with the "draw curves" tool. I resampled the curve to have 64 points at equivalent distance and tranformed points in landmarks with tpsUtil. However according to the specimens the points are not all exactly in the same place even if the starting point is the same, what makes that they are not homologous is that it? So can i use gpagen and other analysis ?

I have attached an example. It is the same place on the molars, the starting point (we do not see it) is the same for the two images but the resampling to have 64 points at the same distance gives points which are not necessarily in the same place. And what I understood is that for morphometric analyzes you had to place the points in the same place...
